sentences: Beneath cold peaks, a snow-covered valley lies perfectly still.
This is Winter Landscape, a Korean hanging scroll painted in the sixteenth century, during the Joseon dynasty.
It is attributed to a painter known only as Yeoseol.
It is painted in ink and slight colour on silk, and the picture itself measures 92.4 centimetres high and 52.7 centimetres wide.
The Cleveland Museum of Art in the United States bought it in 1986 from a collector in Japan.
Look first at the upper right corner.
A small seal is stamped there.
It reads Yeoseol, which means snow-like.
In truth, this seal is almost all we know about the painter; no other record of his life has come down to us.
Now take in the whole picture.
A valley runs diagonally across it, dividing the near scenery from the far.

The museum calls it a vivid example of idealistic, monumental landscape painting, and describes how the dynamic lines and contrasting tones lead our eyes from the lower foreground all the way up to the cold mountain peaks in the distance.
Come down to the nearby scenery at the bottom.
There is someone reading inside a thatched hut, someone crossing a bridge, and someone seeing off a guest.
Even deep in the snowbound mountains, ordinary human days carry on.
Look for a rider and the servant carrying his load.
The painting is almost entirely in monochrome ink, yet the museum points out that the horse's saddle and the servant's carrier still show traces of light blue pigment.
It is a tiny touch of colour hidden in a cold world.
Now look up to the far scenery.
Mist lies thick in the valley beneath the mountains, so that the trees appear only as faint shapes.
The peaks rise sharp and pointed, and the surfaces of the rocks are built up from many short, twisting brushstrokes and dots.
How was the snow painted?
In winter scenes of this period, painters did not usually brush on white.
Instead they left the silk bare and laid ink around it, so that the untouched ground reads as snow.
Here the strong contrasts between dark and pale ink make those empty places glow white.
As a fine example of early Joseon landscape painting, the scroll has travelled back to Korea more than once.

It was shown at the Leeum Museum of Art in Seoul in 2015, in the exhibition Exquisite and Precious, and again in the summer of 2025 at the National Museum of Korea, in its great survey of early Joseon art.
Step back and look once more.
This is the winter of a painter who left us no name, only a seal that says snow-like.
When the first snow falls this winter, you might remember this quiet valley.
